newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS-Mexico's Q1 corp results show weak economy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Mexico's Q1 corp results show weak economy.

text.p: Mexican companies were caught between a rock and a hard place during the first quarter: the peso was too strong to fuel export growth and the economy was not strong enough to help them grow at home.

Recent first quarter results by Mexican firms fell short of expectations in nearly every sector, pouring cold water on hopes the Mexican economy was staging a strong comeback from the 1994-1995 peso crisis, analysts said.
Net profits fell sharply across the board, although that was mostly because companies had slight foreign exchange losses compared to big foreign exchange gains in the year-ago quarter.

Sales slumped by 1.2 percent and operating profits fell on average by 6.9 percent versus the first quarter of 1996, according to a survey of 61 publicly traded companies by Caspian Research in Mexico City.

The peso lost just two percent against the dollar from the first quarter of 1996, but inflation in Mexico ran at nearly 25 percent, making the yearly comparison seem worse as companies restated 1996 earnings according to inflation.

"People were hoping to see some year-on-year rebound in earnings and it didn't happen. Some companies had good growth, but net, net it is a very sloppy market," said Ed Cabrera, chief Latin American strategist at Merrill Lynch in New York.
Exporters that had benefited from a weak peso following the crisis had a harder time selling abroad and saw their dollar revenues translate to fewer pesos in real terms.

Mining companies on average saw their sales plunge some 19 percent during the quarter, although sales fell a more modest 4.7 percent compared to the fourth quarter of 1996, according to the Caspian survey.
Margins at export companies held up well, however, as many firms carried out cost cutting that their domestically focused counterparts had done during much of last year, analysts said.
While the export sector has been slowing down, it appears it is too soon to rely on the local consumer to pick up the slack, analysts said.
"There are no outstanding, clear winners from the current environment," said Damian Fraser, head of analysis at Caspian Research in Mexico City.
Retailers turned in yet another poor quarter with the exception of Soriana, a retailer based in northern Mexico that has benefitted from a faster economic recovery in the industrialized north.
Mexico's largest retailer, Cifra SA, saw its same-store sales fall 4.0 percent compared to the same period of 1996.
"Expectations for a recovery in the consumer sector for the second or third time have run ahead of reality," said Ricardo Peon, chief analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.

Peon added, however, that a lot of temporary conditions made for a worse-than-expected quarter. Lower cigarrette prices to fight contraband hurt conglomerates Grupo Carso and Empresas La Moderna, higher fuel prices and extra capacity in 1996 made for a poor quarter for cement companies, and slow government infrastructure spending pinched construction firms, he said.
And Fraser said profits were also artificially hurt by fewer working days during the quarter because Holy Week fell during March instead of April.
Fraser also said increased competition began to take a toll on some blue-chip companies such as bellwether Telmex, Televisa and retail firms.
Funnily enough, the only bright spot in an otherwise dismal quarter were the banks, who were the hardest hit of all by the 1994-1995 peso crisis.
